findings.control_name: Public Access Block Must Be Enabled
findings.control_description: S3 buckets must have the public access block fully enabled. When disabled, the bucket has no safety net against accidental public exposure from policy or ACL changes. This detects the enabling condition for public access, not the exposure itself.

evidence.temporal_risk: Asset non-compliant for 89712 hours (SLA: 0 hours). Exposed since 2015-10-18T00:00:00Z.

remediation.description: Public Access Block is not fully enabled. The bucket has no safety net against accidental public exposure from policy or ACL changes.
remediation.action: Enable all four Public Access Block settings on the bucket: BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy, RestrictPublicBuckets.

fix_plan.action: Enable all four Public Access Block settings on the bucket: BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy, RestrictPublicBuckets.

violation.control_name: Public Access Block Must Be Enabled

reasoning.clause: all four Public Access Block flags are enabled = false
storage.kind = "bucket"

remediation_context.action: Enable all four Public Access Block settings on the bucket: BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy, RestrictPublicBuckets.

findings.defect: The bucket's Public Access Block is not fully enabled — at least one of BlockPublicAcls, IgnorePublicAcls, BlockPublicPolicy, RestrictPublicBuckets is disabled. The bucket has no catch-all defense against a future ACL or policy change that would expose content publicly.
findings.infection: PAB is a defense-in-depth control: even if the bucket is currently private, any subsequent change to the bucket policy or ACL can make it public with no intermediate warning. PAB, when fully enabled, rejects the change at configuration time — the AWS API returns an error rather than accepting the unsafe policy. Without PAB, operators performing routine maintenance or automation running at scale can accidentally flip a bucket public. Audit trails attribute the exposure to the operator or script, not to the absent safety net, so investigations often miss that PAB-on-everywhere would have prevented the incident.
findings.failure: Future accidental exposure through routine bucket changes. The bucket is not currently public, so this control is preventive, not reactive — the failure it describes is whatever would happen if an unrelated configuration change made the bucket public. Enabling PAB eliminates the class entirely for this bucket regardless of which mechanism (ACL, policy, future API surface) would otherwise have opened the exposure.

findings.control_description: S3 buckets with any non-public data classification must use SSE-KMS encryption with a customer-managed key, not SSE-S3 (AES256). AES256 uses AWS-managed keys with no customer control over key rotation, access policies, or audit trails. This fires on all classified data except explicitly public or non-sensitive buckets.

evidence.temporal_risk: Asset non-compliant for 89712 hours (SLA: 0 hours). Exposed since 2015-10-18T00:00:00Z.

remediation.description: Bucket with classified data is using SSE-S3 (AES256) instead of SSE-KMS. AWS-managed keys provide no customer control over key rotation, access policies, or audit trails.

fix_plan.action: Change the bucket default encryption to SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key. Re-encrypt existing objects by copying them in place with the new encryption settings.

reasoning.clause: the bucket allows anonymous read = true

remediation_context.action: Enable S3 Public Access Block (all four settings). Remove any bucket policy statements granting access to Principal "*". Remove any ACL grants to AllUsers or AuthenticatedUsers.

findings.defect: The bucket's access configuration grants read permission to the public — either via a bucket policy statement with Principal "*" or via an ACL grant to the AllUsers pseudo-group. The bucket is reachable without authentication from the public internet.
findings.infection: Anyone on the internet can fetch objects from this bucket over anonymous HTTP/HTTPS. Search engines and automated scanners continuously enumerate publicly-indexed bucket names, meaning exposure is active from the moment the policy or ACL is in place — not hypothetical. Once the bucket name is known, every object whose key the caller can guess or enumerate is fetchable.
findings.failure: Unbounded data exposure. Every file stored in this bucket is readable by arbitrary internet callers, including potentially sensitive operational data, customer information, backup artifacts, or internal documentation that wasn't intended to reach the public surface.

reasoning.clause: the bucket allows anonymous read = true

remediation_context.action: Enable S3 Public Access Block (all four settings). Remove any bucket policy statements granting access to Principal "*". Remove any ACL grants to AllUsers or AuthenticatedUsers.

findings.defect: The bucket's access configuration grants read permission to the public — either via a bucket policy statement with Principal "*" or via an ACL grant to the AllUsers pseudo-group. The bucket is reachable without authentication from the public internet.
findings.infection: Anyone on the internet can fetch objects from this bucket over anonymous HTTP/HTTPS. Search engines and automated scanners continuously enumerate publicly-indexed bucket names, meaning exposure is active from the moment the policy or ACL is in place — not hypothetical. Once the bucket name is known, every object whose key the caller can guess or enumerate is fetchable.
findings.failure: Unbounded data exposure. Every file stored in this bucket is readable by arbitrary internet callers, including potentially sensitive operational data, customer information, backup artifacts, or internal documentation that wasn't intended to reach the public surface.

reasoning.clause: the bucket allows anonymous write = true

remediation_context.action: Remove bucket policy statements that grant s3:PutObject or s3:DeleteObject to Principal "*". Remove ACL grants that allow WRITE or FULL_CONTROL to AllUsers or AuthenticatedUsers. Enable S3 Public Access Block.

findings.defect: The bucket's composite storage.access.public_write state is true — via bucket ACL (WRITE or FULL_CONTROL to AllUsers or AuthenticatedUsers), via bucket policy (s3:PutObject/Delete/* to Principal "*"), or both. Anonymous callers can upload or delete objects.
findings.infection: Attackers upload arbitrary objects — malware, phishing pages, inflated payloads to exhaust budget, replacement versions of legitimate files — without authenticating. Object-level keys can be chosen to mimic existing content. If the bucket serves a website, CDN origin, or update channel, the attacker- uploaded content propagates to every downstream consumer automatically. Public write also enables ransomware: delete existing objects, re-upload encrypted copies, demand payment for recovery.
findings.failure: Active tampering with bucket contents: injected malicious files, ransomware encryption, or supply-chain compromise when downstream consumers fetch attacker content. Unlike public read (which is passive exposure), public write is active compromise — every new object is a potential incident and the integrity of existing objects cannot be trusted without independent verification.

findings.control_name: No Public Read via Bucket Policy
findings.control_description: S3 bucket policies must not grant read access to an anonymous or wildcard principal. A Statement with Effect Allow, Principal "*" or AWS: "*", and an Action such as s3:GetObject without a restricting Condition enables any unauthenticated caller to read objects. This is distinct from CTL.S3.PUBLIC.001, which fires on the composite public_read signal regardless of mechanism; this control narrows to the bucket-policy path so the finding points the operator at the policy specifically. For ACL-based public read, see CTL.S3.ACL.FULLCONTROL.001 (FULL_CONTROL grants) and CTL.S3.ACL.ESCALATION.001 (WRITE_ACP grants).

evidence.temporal_risk: Asset non-compliant for 89712 hours (SLA: 0 hours). Exposed since 2015-10-18T00:00:00Z.

remediation.description: Bucket policy grants s3:GetObject, s3:GetObjectAcl, or equivalent read action to an anonymous or wildcard principal. Any unauthenticated caller can read objects.
remediation.action: Remove or constrain the policy statement granting read actions to Principal "*" or AWS: "*". If broad read access is genuinely required, add a restricting Condition on aws:PrincipalOrgID, aws:SourceVpc, or a fixed aws:SourceIp CIDR. Enable S3 Public Access Block with BlockPublicPolicy set to true to reject future policies that grant public read.

remediation_context.action: Remove or constrain the policy statement granting read actions to Principal "*" or AWS: "*". findings.defect: The bucket policy contains a Statement with Effect "Allow", Principal "*" (or AWS: "*"), and a read action such as s3:GetObject or s3:GetObjectAcl. No restricting Condition narrows the principal to a specific account, VPC, IP range, or organization.
findings.infection: Any unauthenticated HTTP caller can fetch objects from this bucket. Distinct from ACL-driven exposure in that policy- based public read often applies to specific prefixes or objects, not the whole bucket — but adopters miss the distinction and treat "policy allows public read" as "this bucket is public." Search engines and scanners enumerate buckets via GetBucketPolicy lookups specifically to find policy-granted read access, because it persists even when ACLs are tightened.
findings.failure: Data exposure for objects matched by the policy's Resource clause. Scope depends on whether the policy grants read on the whole bucket (arn:aws:s3:::bucket/*) or a subset — but adopters commonly over-scope the Resource clause during authoring, so "intentional limited public read" often becomes "entire bucket public" in practice. Audit the policy's Resource ARNs to understand exposure surface.

near_miss_chains.description: A resource tagged with a high-sensitivity classification (confidential, restricted, PII, PHI, PCI) is stored in or accessed from an unprotected storage resource — one that is publicly accessible, lacks encryption, or has both. The classification tag declares the data as sensitive; the storage posture contradicts that declaration. Individually the classification and storage controls may pass their own checks; the compound finding is that the two together create a gap.
